title: Abattoir Process Flow and General Processes

lessons.title: From arrival to bleeding
lessons.html:
The first stages of the process

Arrival and offloading

Animals arrive by truck with movement documents and identification. Offloading should be calm, using ramps at a gentle angle with non-slip surfaces. Injured or sick animals are reported immediately. Rough handling causes bruising and stress that lower meat quality and break animal welfare rules under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

Lairage

  • Animals rest in pens with water, shade and enough space.
  • Rest reduces stress and helps restore muscle glycogen, which improves meat quality.
  • Different species, and animals from different sources, are kept apart where needed. Bulls and horned animals may need separate pens.

Ante-mortem inspection

Before slaughter, animals are inspected alive, at rest and in motion, in good light. The inspector looks for signs of disease such as fever, lameness, abnormal breathing, discharges, swellings, nervous signs or abnormal behaviour. Suspect animals are held in the isolation pen for further examination, slaughtered separately at the end of the day, or rejected, according to the inspection decision. Animals that died in transit or lairage are never slaughtered for food.

Stunning

Stunning makes the animal unconscious before bleeding so that it feels no pain. Methods depend on species and include penetrating captive bolt for cattle and electrical stunning for sheep and pigs. The operator checks for effective stunning (no rhythmic breathing, no eye reflex) and restuns immediately if needed. Equipment must be maintained and a backup stunner available.

Bleeding (sticking)

The major blood vessels in the neck or chest are cut promptly after stunning so the animal dies from blood loss before it can regain consciousness. Good bleeding improves meat keeping quality. Knives are sterilised between animals.

Safety

Stunning equipment, kicking animals and sharp knives are serious hazards. Only trained operators stun, captive bolt guns are never pointed at people, and workers wear protective equipment.

lessons.title: Dressing, inspection, chilling and dispatch
lessons.html:
Turning the animal into a carcass

Dressing

Dressing removes the hide, head, feet and internal organs under hygienic conditions. General steps for cattle and sheep:

  1. Head and feet removal, with heads identified so they can be matched to the carcass for inspection.
  2. Hide removal (flaying): opening cuts made from the inside outward so hair is not pulled into the meat; the outer surface of the hide must not touch the carcass.
  3. Rodding the gullet and bunging the rectum (tying or sealing) to stop leakage.
  4. Evisceration: removal of the stomach, intestines and other organs without puncturing the gut. Organs (offal) stay identified with their carcass.
  5. Splitting of cattle carcasses into sides with a saw.

Pigs are commonly scalded and dehaired instead of skinned, then singed and scraped.

Post-mortem inspection

The meat inspector or examiner inspects the head, offal and carcass at set points, by looking, feeling and making incisions into specific lymph nodes and organs as the procedures require. Findings decide whether parts or the whole carcass are passed, partially condemned, detained for further examination or condemned. Detained carcasses go onto a separate rail.

Trimming, washing and grading

Visible contamination and damage are trimmed off. Carcasses may be washed with clean water. Carcasses are classified and marked (for example by age and fatness classes) and weighed. Approved carcasses receive the official inspection stamp.

Chilling

Carcasses enter chillers promptly, hung with space between them for air flow. Temperatures are monitored. Chilling slows bacterial growth and firms the meat for handling.

Dispatch

Meat is loaded into clean, refrigerated vehicles once it reaches the required temperature, with documents for traceability.

By-products

Hides, edible offal, tripe, blood and inedible material are processed in their own areas, never mixed with carcass meat.

Key points

  • Calm offloading and rest in lairage protect welfare and meat quality.
  • Ante-mortem inspection identifies sick animals before slaughter.
  • Stunning must be effective; bleed promptly after stunning.
  • Dress hygienically, keep offal identified with its carcass.
  • Post-mortem inspection decides if meat is passed, detained or condemned.

quiz.question: Why do animals rest in the lairage before slaughter?

options.text: To reduce stress and help restore muscle glycogen

quiz.question: What happens to an animal that died in the lairage?

options.text: It is sold as pet food at the gate
It is never slaughtered for food
It is chilled with other carcasses

quiz.question: Which sign shows that stunning was NOT effective?
Why must offal stay identified with its carcass?

options.text: So inspection findings can be linked to the right carcass
